sentences.text: An hour and forty minutes is a great deal of time and Fuentelosa used every minute of it, and everybody in that village would have told you they were simply getting on with things.
The bread came out at about the fortieth minute.

Rocío's grandmother had run those ovens since 1979 and could have told you the time by what stage the second batch was at, and she was, by some distance, the person in Fuentelosa who understood the morning best and thought about it least.

Rocío's grandmother had been at the ovens since before the lark went up and the queue formed at about half past six and stood in the road for the better part of an hour, and the queue was not a queue in the sense of people waiting to buy bread.
It was where the village found out what had happened.
Somebody's water.
Somebody's roof.
A tractor for sale.
Whose son was back from Bilbao and for how long.
The whole of it, every day, in the road, in the dark going grey, with the lark up above the barley and nobody in any hurry at all.
The old men were on the wall by the fountain from about the fiftieth minute.

That is not a figure of speech either — Rocío timed them for a fortnight and it was between forty-eight and fifty-five, every day, four of them, and they sat there until the lark came down and then they got up and went and did something.
The school did not open until the ninetieth minute.
It has done since 1974 and there is a memo about it in a drawer that gives a reason to do with the bus that has not been true since 1991.

And her mother and her aunt walked to the cemetery on Thursdays, which took an hour there and back with the standing about, and which fitted into the morning exactly and would not have fitted into a morning of fifty-five minutes, and which is a thing they had both done every Thursday for nineteen years without either of them ever describing it as anything.
None of this was arranged.
That is what Rocío has never been able to get anybody to see.
Nobody in Fuentelosa sat down in 1950 and allocated the morning.
It had simply grown into the space, the way a plant grows into a pot, and the pot was an hour and forty minutes wide.
And because nobody had arranged it, nobody could see it.
Every single one of those things had a reason that had nothing to do with the length of anything.
The bread queue was long because people are friendly.
The men were on the wall because they were old.
The school opened late because of a bus in 1974.
Ask anybody in that village why the morning was the length it was and they would have looked at you as though you had asked why the road was the length it was.
